text:
A pace plan treats the body like an engine that never changes, but the body actually runs on a fuel tank.

A trained runner stores roughly 400 to 500 grams of glycogen in the muscles and liver. That is about 2,000 calories. Marathon pace burns close to 100 calories per mile, so the tank runs dry somewhere near mile 20.

After that, the body has to rely on fat oxidation, which delivers ATP more slowly. Suppose a runner gained a few seconds early on, running a cool, flat first half faster than planned. That runner now finds the fuel account overdrawn. The splits that felt sustainable at mile 12 demand power the body can no longer release.

Other problems add to the shortfall:
- Heat
- Dehydration that costs two percent of body mass
- Eccentric quad damage

Then the wall arrives.

To prevent it:
- Run negative splits, with a disciplined start.
- Take in 60 to 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour.
- Do long runs that train the body to burn fat before race day.
